t: Contraception, emergency contraception and medication abortion
sub: Every method blocks one step between a growing follicle and an implanted embryo, and estrogen, not progestin, carries most of the serious risk.

pretest.q: A woman cannot safely take estrogen. Which kind of hormonal contraception can she still use?
pretest.why: The progestin blocks the LH surge, thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium on its own, so the minipill, the DMPA injection, the implant and the levonorgestrel IUD all work without estrogen.

w.A combined oral pill: Combined pills contain ethinyl estradiol, which raises hepatic clotting factors, so they carry exactly the risk she must avoid.
w.The transdermal patch: The patch delivers ethinyl estradiol through the skin and gives even higher estrogen exposure than most pills, so clot risk is not reduced.
w.The vaginal ring: The ring releases ethinyl estradiol with etonogestrel, so it shares every estrogen contraindication with the pill and the patch.

pretest.q: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception mainly works by which action?
pretest.why: A single high dose of levonorgestrel postpones the LH surge, so the follicle does not rupture while sperm are still alive. It has no effect once a pregnancy has implanted, so it is not an abortifacient.

w.Blocking implantation: Implantation happens about a week after ovulation, and good evidence shows levonorgestrel does not stop an embryo from attaching.
w.Ending an early pregnancy: Ending an implanted pregnancy requires mifepristone and misoprostol; levonorgestrel given after implantation leaves the pregnancy intact.
w.Killing sperm in the uterus: Toxicity to sperm and ova is how the copper IUD works; levonorgestrel acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary instead.

pretest.q: Which drug is given first in a medication abortion?
pretest.why: Mifepristone blocks progesterone receptors, so the decidua breaks down and the uterus becomes sensitive to prostaglandins. Misoprostol follows 24 to 48 hours later to contract the uterus and expel the tissue.

w.Misoprostol: Misoprostol is the second drug; it works far better once mifepristone has withdrawn progesterone support and primed the myometrium.
w.Methotrexate: Methotrexate kills rapidly dividing trophoblast and is the medical treatment for a small ectopic pregnancy, not the standard first drug.
w.Oxytocin: Oxytocin receptors are scarce in the early pregnant uterus, so oxytocin is used for labor and postpartum bleeding instead.

body: How do estrogen and progestin each prevent pregnancy?

Hormonal contraception borrows the ovary's own brake. A steady dose of hormone keeps **negative feedback** on the hypothalamus and pituitary switched on, so GnRH pulses slow and FSH and LH stay low. The two hormones in {{rp10_chc|combined hormonal contraception}} then split the work. Estrogen blunts FSH, so no follicle becomes dominant, and it keeps the endometrium stable, which gives predictable bleeding. The progestin blocks the **LH surge**, so ovulation does not happen; it also thickens **cervical mucus** so sperm cannot swim through, and it thins the endometrium. Because the progestin does most of the contraceptive work, a method can drop estrogen and still prevent pregnancy; what it loses is a regular bleeding pattern.
Suppresses FSH, so no follicle becomes dominant
Stabilizes the endometrium; raises SHBG, so free testosterone and acne fall
Venous and arterial clots, because the liver makes more clotting factors
Blocks the LH surge and thickens cervical mucus
Thins the endometrium; irregular spotting when used alone
Bone loss with DMPA; acne with androgenic progestins
Every hormonal method contains a progestin

The progestin is the part that reliably stops ovulation and blocks sperm, so every hormonal method carries one. Estrogen is added for **cycle control**, and it is the source of the clotting and cardiovascular risk. When estrogen is unsafe, the answer is a progestin-only or nonhormonal method, never no contraception.
Which methods contain estrogen, and which work best in real life?

Methods fall into three families. The pill, the weekly **transdermal patch** and the monthly **vaginal ring** all combine ethinyl estradiol with a progestin. The progestin-only family is the minipill, the DMPA injection, the etonogestrel implant and the levonorgestrel IUD. The copper IUD, condoms, the diaphragm and sterilization use no hormone. Effectiveness depends less on the molecule than on how much the method relies on the user. With {{rp10_typical|typical use}}, about 7 in 100 pill, patch or ring users become pregnant each year, mostly from missed doses, while fewer than 1 in 100 implant or IUD users do. That is why {{rp10_larc|long-acting reversible contraception}} is offered first to anyone who wants it, adolescents included.

Barrier methods and sterilization use no hormone. The male condom fails in about 13 in 100 couples a year with typical use, and it is the only method here that also lowers the risk of sexually transmitted infection, so it is paired with a more effective method. The **diaphragm**, placed over the cervix with spermicide, fails in about 17 in 100. Sterilization is permanent: women have the tubes occluded or removed, and men have a **vasectomy**, which cuts the vas deferens, with a semen analysis after about 3 months to confirm that no sperm remain. The gap between **perfect use** and typical use shows how much a method depends on the user: the pill fails in about 0.3 per 100 with perfect use but about 7 with typical use, whereas an implant or IUD fails in under 1 either way.

Estrogen raises the liver's output of clotting factors, so every estrogen-containing method raises the risk of **venous thromboembolism**, and in susceptible women the risk of stroke and myocardial infarction. The contraindications follow from that: a smoker over 35, **migraine with aura**, prior VTE or stroke, known thrombophilia, ischemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, fewer than 21 days postpartum, and severe liver disease or hepatic adenoma. Current breast cancer rules out every hormonal method, so a copper IUD is used. The same pills bring real benefits: lighter, regular, less painful periods, less acne and hirsutism, and a lower lifetime risk of ovarian cancer and endometrial cancer.
Rifampin defeats the pill; amoxicillin does not

Only drugs that induce hepatic CYP3A4 lower contraceptive hormone levels: **rifampin**, carbamazepine, phenytoin, topiramate and St John's wort. Ordinary antibiotics such as amoxicillin or doxycycline do not. A woman who needs a long course of an {{rp10_inducer|enzyme inducer}} is steered to DMPA, whose high dose outlasts faster metabolism, or to an IUD, which acts locally.
Why do combined pills lower the risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer?

Each ovulation tears the ovarian surface and the nearby tubal epithelium, and every repair is another chance for a mutation. By suppressing ovulation, combined pills cut the number of lifetime ovulations, so ovarian cancer risk falls by roughly a third, more with longer use, and the protection lasts decades after stopping. Endometrial cancer is driven by estrogen acting without progesterone. Every active pill contains a progestin, which keeps the lining thin and secretory, so the endometrium never sees **unopposed estrogen**; its cancer risk falls by a similar amount and also persists long after the pills stop.
How are the combined methods used, and why does bleeding break through?
Daily: 21 to 24 active pills, then 4 to 7 hormone-free days with a withdrawal bleed
Extended or continuous packs skip the bleed
Replaced weekly for 3 weeks, then 1 week off
Higher estrogen exposure than most pills; less reliable above about 90 kg or a BMI of 30
In place for 3 weeks, out for 1
Irritation or expulsion are the common reasons to stop

Any method can start on any day once pregnancy is reasonably excluded, which is called quick start. Within the first 5 days of a period it protects at once; otherwise condoms are used for the first 7 days, or 2 days for the minipill. One missed active pill is taken as soon as it is remembered. Two or more missed in a row can let a follicle escape suppression, so take the most recent missed pill, use condoms for 7 days, and offer emergency contraception if unprotected sex followed missed pills early in the pack.

{{rp10_btb|Breakthrough bleeding}}, unscheduled bleeding or spotting while taking active hormone, is the most common adverse effect of every hormonal method. It is most frequent in the first 3 months, while the endometrium adapts, and settles in most users. Estrogen stabilizes the lining, so low-dose, progestin-only and continuous regimens bleed more, as do missed pills, smoking and enzyme inducers that lower hormone levels. Bleeding that persists beyond the first months prompts a pregnancy test and a check for chlamydia, cervicitis or a polyp before the product is changed. Other estrogen effects are nausea, breast tenderness and headache; progestin effects are mood change, acne and, with DMPA, weight gain.
How do progestin-only methods and IUDs differ?

Progestin-only methods avoid estrogen's clot risk, so they suit women with estrogen contraindications and women who are breastfeeding, but they trade away predictable bleeding. The minipill relies mostly on cervical mucus, so it must be taken at the same time each day, and fertility returns as soon as it stops. Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (**DMPA**), injected every 3 months, suppresses ovulation strongly; amenorrhea is common, weight gain is typical, bone density falls during use, and fertility can take many months to return. The etonogestrel **implant**, a rod under the skin of the arm, lasts 3 years and is the most effective reversible method, but it causes unpredictable spotting. The **levonorgestrel** IUD thins the endometrium from inside the uterus, so periods lighten or stop, which makes it a first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding.

The copper IUD contains no hormone. Copper ions provoke a sterile inflammatory reaction in the uterus that is toxic to sperm and ova, so fertilization rarely happens. It works for 10 years or more, but periods often become heavier and more painful. Any IUD insertion carries a small risk of **pelvic infection** in the first few weeks, because bacteria from the cervix can be carried upward, so active pelvic inflammatory disease or purulent cervicitis is treated before insertion. Pregnancy and a distorted uterine cavity also rule an IUD out.
Must be taken on time; fertility returns at once
Bone density loss; slow return of fertility
How does emergency contraception differ from medication abortion?

**Emergency contraception** works before implantation, by delaying ovulation or by stopping fertilization, so it cannot end a pregnancy that has already implanted and is not an **abortifacient**. Levonorgestrel, a single high dose of progestin, works best within 72 hours and only if it is taken before the LH surge begins; it also loses efficacy as **body mass index** rises, from about a BMI of 30. Ulipristal, a {{rp10_sprm|selective progesterone receptor modulator}}, works for up to 5 days, can still delay follicle rupture after LH has started to rise, and is less affected by weight, so it outperforms levonorgestrel late in the window and in obesity. A copper IUD placed within 5 days is the most effective option of all, is not affected by weight, and then keeps working as ongoing contraception.

Medication abortion ends a pregnancy that has already implanted, so its two drugs act after implantation. **Mifepristone** is a progesterone receptor antagonist: without progesterone's support, the decidua breaks down, the pregnancy detaches, the cervix softens and the myometrium becomes sensitive to prostaglandins. **Misoprostol**, a prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) analog given 24 to 48 hours later, then drives strong uterine contractions and ripens the cervix to expel the tissue. Cramping and bleeding heavier than a period are expected effects, and misoprostol often adds nausea, diarrhea, fever and chills. As of 2025 the regimen is approved through 70 days of gestation: mifepristone 200 mg by mouth, then misoprostol 800 mcg buccally.
Confirm an intrauterine pregnancy and its age
The regimen does not treat an ectopic pregnancy, so the location and gestational age are confirmed first, by history and by ultrasound when needed.

Blocking progesterone receptors breaks down the decidua and softens the cervix. The drug also blocks glucocorticoid receptors, so chronic adrenal failure and long-term steroid therapy are contraindications.
Given 24 to 48 hours later, the prostaglandin E1 analog contracts the myometrium, so cramping and heavy bleeding follow within hours.
A falling hCG or an ultrasound confirms that the pregnancy has passed; retained tissue is treated with more misoprostol or with uterine aspiration.
How is a method chosen and counseled?

Counseling starts with what the patient wants: when she may want pregnancy, how she feels about bleeding changes, and whether she can use estrogen. A sexual history covers partners, practices, protection from infection, past infections and pregnancy intention, the five Ps; pregnancy intention opens the contraceptive conversation, and asking in the practices step whether sex is consensual identifies coercion. Only condoms also prevent sexually transmitted infection. An **adolescent** can consent to contraception without a parent in most states, so part of the visit is held alone and kept **confidential**, with the limits of confidentiality explained first. No pelvic examination is needed before starting pills, a patch, a ring, an injection or an implant. Each method's pitfall follows from what it does, so the choice matches her history and medicines to the pitfalls below.

body.q: A woman had unprotected sex 3 days ago, and a home LH test turned positive yesterday. Which reasoning best explains why levonorgestrel is a poor choice?
o: Levonorgestrel works by blocking implantation, and implantation has already happened three days after intercourse
Levonorgestrel only delays ovulation if taken before the LH surge begins, so once LH is rising it cannot stop follicle rupture
Levonorgestrel would end a pregnancy that has started, so it is avoided once fertilization may have occurred
Levonorgestrel needs estrogen to suppress FSH, and a single progestin dose cannot do that in time
body.why: Levonorgestrel emergency contraception works by postponing the LH surge, so it helps only while the follicle is still waiting for that signal. A positive LH test means the surge has begun, and the follicle will rupture about 36 hours later whatever progestin is given. Implantation happens about a week after ovulation, not three days after intercourse, and levonorgestrel does not disturb it. Ulipristal can still delay rupture after LH starts rising, and a copper IUD blocks fertilization, so either is the better choice.
